When your goal is to bring down heating costs, you should concentrate first on the building envelope and then on the heating system and controls.  Even without specific EPC values on hand, the general hierarchy of measures looks like this:

1. Improve insulation and airtightness  
   • Roof/attic and exterior-wall insulation have some of the quickest paybacks.  
   • Insulate basement or ground-floor slabs if they are uninsulated.  
   • Seal drafts around windows, doors and service penetrations (air-taping, weather-stripping).  

2. Upgrade windows and exterior doors  
   • Install high-performance, energy-efficient windows (double or triple glazing with low-e coatings).  
   • Ensure frames and seals are tight.  

3. Optimize or replace the heating plant  
   • If you have an old oil or standard gas boiler, consider a high-efficiency condensing boiler or – even better – an air- or ground-source heat pump.  
   • Correctly size the new equipment to your (improved) building heat demand

However, “point-of-use efficiency” is only part of the story. Key considerations are:

1. Operating Cost  
 • Electricity is generally one of the most expensive heating fuels by kWh. Even though you get all the input energy back as heat, your utility bill will typically be higher than with gas-fired boilers, district heating or air-source heat pumps.  
 • If you benefit from a low-tariff electricity period (off-peak or so-called “night storage” tariffs), costs can be somewhat reduced—but the radiators must run during that window to maximize savings.

Here are some best practices for getting the most efficient, comfortable performance from direct-acting electric radiators:

1. Fit a room thermostat or programmable timer  
   • A dedicated room thermostat lets each radiator switch itself on/off to maintain your set-point (rather than running flat-out).  
   • A 24-hour programmer (or “week timer”) allows you to reduce temperature whenever rooms are unoccupied or you’re asleep.  

2. Use thermostatic radiator valves (TRVs) or built-in controls  
   • TRVs on each unit let you adjust heat output per room. Keep corridors and bedrooms cooler than living areas.

3. Zone your heating

Energy-efficiency improvement refers to any measure or upgrade that reduces a building’s energy consumption—while maintaining or improving its level of comfort and functionality. In the context of buildings and Energy Performance Certificates (EPCs), this typically means:

1. Building Envelope Upgrades  
    • Insulation (walls, roof, floors): reduces heat losses in winter and heat gains in summer.  
    • High-performance windows and doors: minimizes drafts and thermal bridging.

2. Heating, Ventilation and Air-Conditioning (HVAC) Enhancements  
    • Modern, high-efficiency boilers or heat pumps: convert energy to heat more effectively.  
    • Smart controls and thermostats: optimize temperatures and schedules to match occupancy.  
    • Heat recovery ventilation: recovers heat from exhaust air to pre-warm incoming fresh air.

3. Lighting and Electrical Systems  
    • LED or other high-efficiency lighting fixtures: use significantly less electricity for the same light output.

In Sweden the term “premises” (lokaler) covers any distinct use-area within a property.  When you assess a building’s energy performance—e.g. in an Energy Performance Certificate (EPC)—you first identify and quantify each premise type, because each has its own typical energy profile.  The principal categories are:

1. Residential premises  
   • Apartments or single-family units  
   • Characterized by space heating, domestic hot water, cooking, household appliances and lighting  
   • High variability depending on occupant behaviour and hot-water demand  

2. Office and administration premises  
   • Open-plan offices, individual offices, meeting rooms, reception areas  
   • Significant internal gains from computers, servers and lighting  
   • Often higher ventilation rates; heating and cooling loads depend on occupancy schedules  

3. Retail and service premises  
   • Shops, supermarkets, hair salons, banks, etc.  
   • Intensive lighting demand; in some cases refrigeration or air

1. Lighting (50–70 %)

Natural (or “passive”) ventilation relies on wind pressure and thermal buoyancy (the stack effect) to move fresh air through a building, rather than mechanical fans or ductwork.  Compared with mechanical ventilation, the principal advantages of natural ventilation are:

• Lower energy use and operating cost  
  – No or very little electricity is required to drive fans.  
  – Reduced building energy consumption helps to lower utility bills and operating expenses.  

• Simplicity and reliability  
  – Fewer moving parts (no fans, filters or complex ductwork) mean less can go wrong.  
  – Reduced maintenance requirements and associated service costs.  

• Improved resilience  
  – Continues to operate during power outages or equipment failures.  
  – Particularly valuable in remote locations or in buildings aiming for high sustainability.  

• Enhanced indoor environmental quality  
  – Occupants often perceive naturally ventilated spaces as more pleasant, with a stronger connection to ou

Optimizing natural ventilation in a house is fundamentally about harnessing both wind-driven and buoyancy (stack) effects to create controlled air flows without mechanical fans. Below are design and operational strategies you can apply:

1. Site and Orientation  
  • Analyze prevailing wind directions and sun paths. Orient the long axis of the house perpendicular to the dominant wind to maximize cross­-ventilation.  
  • Incorporate landscaping (rows of trees or shrubs) to channel or diffuse winds as needed.

2. Window and Opening Placement  
  • Cross-Ventilation: Place operable windows or vents on opposite or adjacent façades so air can enter on the windward side and exit on the leeward side.  
  • Stack Ventilation: Create high and low openings (e.g. lower windows or vents plus roof vents, clerestory windows or skylights). Warm air rises and escapes through the high outlet, drawing cooler outside air in through the lower inlet.

Control and regulation technology (sometimes called “building automation” or “styr-/reglerteknik” in Swedish) refers to the combination of sensors, controllers, actuators and software that together measure, monitor and automatically adjust a building’s technical systems so as to maintain comfort, safety and energy efficiency.  

Key elements include  
• Sensors – devices that continuously measure environmental parameters such as temperature, humidity, air quality, pressure or light levels.  
• Controllers – electronic units (for example PLCs or dedicated regulator modules) that compare each sensor’s feedback to a pre-set desired value (setpoint) and calculate how much adjustment is needed.  
• Actuators – valves, dampers, variable-speed drives, relays or motors that actually open, close, speed up or slow down heating, cooling, ventilation, lighting or shading systems.

In the EV-charging world the terms “normal” (or “slow”) charging and “fast” (or “rapid”) charging are generally distinguished by the power level (kW) delivered and by whether the car is charged with alternating current (AC) or direct current (DC).  Below is a summary of the most commonly used categories:

1. Slow (“normal”) AC charging  
   • Power: up to about 3.7 kW (single-phase)  
   • Typical use: home wall-outlets (Mode 2) or basic wallboxes (Mode 3)  
   • Charge rate: adds roughly 10–15 km of range per hour  

2. Fast AC charging (sometimes still called “normal” by charging-station vendors)  
   • Power: 3.7 – 22 kW (three-phase, Mode 3)  
   • Typical use: home wallboxes (higher-capacity), workplaces, public on-street stations  
   • Charge rate: adds roughly 20–80 km of range per hour, depending on vehicle  

3. DC fast (rapid) charging  
   • Power: generally from 25 kW up to 350 kW (Mode 4)  
   • Typical use: highway-side “corridor” chargers, commercial charging hubs

Load balancing for EV charging is a smart-charging technique that ensures the total electrical load drawn by one or more electric vehicle (EV) chargers stays within the limits of the building’s or site’s electrical installation and the utility grid. By actively monitoring and adjusting charging power, load balancing helps to:

1. Prevent overloads and nuisance tripping  
   – Avoids exceeding the fuse or breaker capacity of the building’s main supply.  
   – Reduces the risk of voltage dips that could affect other electrical equipment.

2. Optimize use of available capacity

In most national and international lighting standards (for example SS-EN 12464-1), stairwells and other internal circulation areas are given the following recommendations:

• Normal (everyday) lighting  
  – Maintained horizontal illuminance on the walking surface: ≥ 100 lx

In special situations – for example elderly care or where vision is impaired – you may choose to increase the normal illuminance to 150–200 lx. Always verify any additional local building-code requirements (e.g. Boverkets byggregler in Sweden) before final design.

Improving illumination in basement spaces requires a combination of daylight‐harvesting (where possible), efficient artificial light sources, thoughtful fixture selection and proper controls. Below are a series of measures you can apply:

1. Introduce or enhance daylighting  
   • Window wells and light shafts – If the basement is partially below grade, install or enlarge window wells or light tubes (“sun tunnels”) to bring in natural light.  
   • Light pipes or fiber systems – In heavily buried areas you can use reflective light‐pipe technology to channel daylight from roof level down into the basement.  

2. Layer artificial lighting  
   • Ambient/general lighting – Use high‐efficiency LED panels or surface-mounted fixtures to deliver a uniform base level (e.g. 200–300 lux for storage or circulation, 300–500 lux for work areas).  
   • Task lighting – Over workbenches, laundry sinks or desks, install directed LED strip lights or adjustable downlights to reach 500–800 lux where need

In Sweden there is no explicit “one‐size‐fits‐all” statutory temperature for stairwells, but by practice and in line with Boverket’s BBR and AMA VVS design guidelines you should use the following as a rule of thumb:

• Minimum temperature to avoid moisture/frost damage: 12 °C  
• Normal design (dimensioning) temperature: 15 °C  

– The 12 °C limit ensures that you do not get condensation or frost on structural elements and avoids very cold drafts.  
– In most multi‐family or public buildings you dimension the heating system for about 15 °C in corridors and stairwells.  

If the stairwell is also used as an escape route or as a quasi‐public area, some designers choose to raise the design temperature to around 16–18 °C for user comfort, but this is not a strict requirement.
